📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery.
  • It has been revealed that the discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that long before a mammal is born, its skin begins establishing the precise locations where hair will eventually grow. These developing hair follicles form intricate geometric arrangements that differ from species to species. But what determines where each follicle appears, and how does the body create such orderly patterns?

It has been revealed that researchers at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) have identified a surprisingly simple process that may help explain this biological mystery. By studying how cells move in response to chemical signals, the team developed a model that successfully recreates the formation of hair follicle patterns in two mammalian species. Their findings, published in PNAS, suggest that elaborate biological structures can emerge naturally from basic interactions between neighboring cells.

It has been revealed that the discovery could help explain a much broader phenomenon in nature. Hair, feathers, and most types of scales begin as small structures called placodes that appear during embryonic development. Scientists have spent decades investigating how these early structures establish the distinctive arrangements seen across different animal species.

Challenging a Long-Standing Theory of Hair Growth.

For laboratory mice (Mus musculus), the leading explanation has traditionally been the expansion-induction model. This theory proposes that when a newly introduced placode appears, it releases a chemical that prevents additional placodes from developing too close to it.

As the embryo's skin grows and stretches, some areas move far enough away from existing placodes to escape the chemical's influence. Upcoming placodes can then develop in those spaces, gradually creating a more complete pattern across the skin.

Although this explanation has gained widespread acceptance, scientists have not experimentally established that it can account for the diversity of follicle patterns found across species.

A Simpler Mechanism for Hair Follicle Formation.

To investigate another possibility, researchers led by Athanasia Tzika, Senior Lecturer, and Michel Milinkovitch, Professor, both in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE's Faculty of Science, focused on a process called chemotaxis.

Chemotaxis occurs when cells move in response to differences in chemical concentrations. The same basic process helps guide white blood cells toward areas of inflammation, allowing the immune system to respond where it is needed.

Sources indicate that the researchers created a mathematical model that tracks how mobile cells in the dermis interact with an attracting chemical signal released by the epidermis, the skin's outer layer. They then simulated the growth of embryonic skin to see whether these interactions could produce the gradual appearance of placodes.

In a recent development, remarkably, the model recreated the developmental patterns observed in laboratory mice, including the same sequence of follicle formation that scientists had previously explained using the expansion-induction theory. This suggests that a complex system of instructions may not be necessary to determine where follicles develop.

Industry observers note that "Our findings show that the observed patterns do not require a complex system telling each placode where to form," explain Muhamet Ibrahimi and Ebrahim Jahanbakhsh, researchers in the Department of Genetics and Evolution. "Instead, placodes emerge spontaneously from local interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

One Simple Process Creates Different Hair Patterns.

The team next investigated whether the same mechanism could explain follicle arrangements in another mammal with a very different coat structure.

They selected the spiny mouse (Acomys dimidiatus), a rodent whose hair follicles develop in an unusually regular pattern with a strong directional alignment. This distinctive organization cannot be explained by the traditional expansion-induction model.

Using experimental information gathered from three-dimensional images of developing embryonic skin, the researchers adapted their simulations to reflect the spiny mouse's particular biochemical characteristics and the way its skin grows.

In a recent development, the results revealed that the same underlying process of cells responding to chemical signals could also reproduce the spiny mouse's highly organized follicle pattern. The differences between the two species could be explained by variations in their cellular interactions, chemical properties, and skin growth rather than entirely different mechanisms.

These findings suggest that the remarkable variety of structures found throughout the animal kingdom may arise from a shared set of relatively simple biological rules. By adjusting how cells interact and respond to their surroundings, nature can generate dramatically different patterns without requiring a separate developmental blueprint for every species.

"Our work suggests that simple cellular interactions can generate the remarkable diversity of tissue architectures observed throughout evolution," concludes Athanasia Tzika. "The differences observed between species therefore result from the same self-organization process, but with variations in the interactions between cells and chemical signals.".

#160. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1599 w)
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily

Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered latest clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Sources indicate that heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered latest clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Sources indicate that heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an crucial role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," states Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

It has been revealed that cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form rapidly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

Industry observers note that all three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

According to recent reports, the researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Sources indicate that because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

According to recent reports, the latest investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Recent findings suggest that researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns indicated substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL revealed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an crucial distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

It has been revealed that all three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

Sources indicate that TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

It has been revealed that lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

Industry observers note that by identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

According to recent reports, "Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Recent findings suggest that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

#159. California's brand-latest Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space

California's brand-latest Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov.
  • According to recent reports, after more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive upcoming wing.
  • According to recent reports, "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).

According to recent reports, after more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive upcoming wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour, sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.

According to recent reports, "It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

"There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience.".

Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the newly introduced wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.

There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.

As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.

You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).

This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.

"I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk.".

Sources indicate that but you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.

However, due to the excitement over this fresh center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. Many Americans are feeling the strain of rising grocery prices, a reality that can make planning for food-focused holidays feel extra stressful. But there are some ways to stretch your dollars and still celebrate with a delicious meal.

#157. How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

How to Make Sure an 'Onion' Site on the Dark Web Is Legitimate

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the dark web isn't just for illicit activities.
  • But this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious users.
  • Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the dark web isn't just for illicit activities. In fact, many legitimate online platforms maintain a ".onion" domain on the dark web for privacy reasons, including media outlets like ProPublica and BBC News, social media sites like Facebook, and privacy-conscious communication platforms like Proton Mail and SecureDrop.

But this also provides perfect cover for criminals and hackers who create clones of legitimate dark web sites to steal sensitive data and cryptocurrency from privacy-conscious users. And given that onion links are long and jumbled, it’s easy for users to accidentally click on the wrong link and end up on a fake website instead of the real one. When the FBI seized 276 onion addresses during 2014's Operation Onymous, they found that 153 of them were phishing sites.

Thankfully, Tor Browser already has a cryptography-backed feature that can verify the authenticity of an onion site, by confirming whether it has end-to-end encryption and extended validation certificates. Here's how this feature works, where it falters, as well as what other red flags you should look for.

It has been revealed that while phishing on the dark web works as it does on the clear web, scammers have a few unique advantages due to the secretive nature of the environment. Most importantly, you can’t just glance at an onion link to tell if the site is genuine. Normal website URLs tend to be short and memorable, while onion links are 56-character strings of alphanumeric text that look mostly like gibberish.

In a recent development, when you try to connect, Tor Browser verifies the URL against the originating website’s cryptographic key, which is how you know nobody has hijacked the address or tampered with it midway. But since this has the unwanted effect of making domains harder to recall, scammers have a much easier time generating lookalike addresses or creating website clones.

It has been revealed that for example, many popular websites use “vanity prefixes” to make their onion addresses more easily identifiable or to add some branding appeal. That means their 56-character onion link starts with something like “facebook,” “bbcnews,” or “ciadotgov.” But scammers can use a free tool like mkp224o to generate lookalike addresses with the same vanity prefix as the legitimate website, which gives users a false sense of security.

Of course, most dark web owners don’t type addresses directly into Tor Browser; they use dark web directories like the Hidden Wiki to find useful onion sites relevant to their search. Scammers will create fake search engines or link directories to point users to their fake websites, like when the Ahmia search engine discovered that a copy of its platform was directing users to 255 cloned services back in 2015.

Of course, it’s possible to orchestrate phishing attempts that don’t involve cloning sites at all. Researchers at Freie Universität Berlin describe a sophisticated technique where attackers serve the real website through their own reverse proxy, which lets them manipulate parts of the site or log your online activity without your awareness. In 2019, ESET even found a trojanized version of Tor Browser that replaced Bitcoin addresses on websites to direct payments to hackers. So both genuine websites and your browser itself are also vulnerable to manipulation if you download or access them from an unverified source.

Industry observers note that there are a few best practices to avoid phishing attacks when using the dark web. None of them are foolproof on their own, but together, they considerably lower the risk of ending up on a fake or manipulated website.

According to recent reports, the Tor Project has a feature called Onion-Location, which lets clear web websites advertise that they have a dark web version available for customers who prefer more privacy. If opening a regular TLS-backed website using the Tor Browser reveals a purple “onion available” button in the address bar, you can click on it and be redirected to the official onion link associated with that site.

Sources indicate that on the desktop version of Tor Browser, you can access an onion site using a shortened version of its URL called an Onion Name. For now, this feature only works with SecureDrop, so newsrooms can establish tip lines with addresses like mysitename.securedrop.tor.onion, which would then redirect to the 56-character original onion address. This feature is in active development, so more platforms might support it in the future.

It has been revealed that when you load up an onion site using the Tor Browser, you’ll see an onion icon on the address bar, which confirms that your connection is end-to-end encrypted. But you can also click on the onion icon to check if the site has an Extended Validation (EV) certificate, which tells you that its authenticity has been verified by a trusted certificate authority like DigiCert. While not every legitimate onion site will have an EV certificate, famous ones like Facebook tend to.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, if you see a caution sign next to the onion icon, that means the site is using a self-signed or expired certificate that isn’t guaranteed by a trusted authority. It may also imply that the site is being served over an insecure URL. This doesn’t definitely tell you it’s a phishing site, but it’s a red flag to watch out for nevertheless.

Industry observers note that don’t rely on search engines, link directories, Reddit threads, or Telegram channels too heavily on the dark web. Once you’re sure you’ve found the onion address for a genuine site, bookmark it so you can access it directly the next time you want to visit.

If you realized that you’ve been the victim of a phishing attempt, the first step is to close the browser window with the fake site and access the real onion address to reset any account passwords you may have accidentally divulged.

Also, generally try to enable two-factor authentication and PGP logins on any dark web account that supports it for added security. And if you downloaded Tor Browser from anywhere other than the official Tor Project site, uninstall it now and grab a fresh copy from the official address.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae.
  • According to recent reports, although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an ancient rodent of extraordinary size has been identified from fossils uncovered in a mine in southern Thailand. The discovery, made by an international team of paleontologists that includes scientists from McGill University, provides upcoming evidence that giant rodents appeared much earlier and in more parts of the world than previously believed.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found "remarkably large" fossilized teeth belonging to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae. This prehistoric rodent lived approximately 34 million years ago, during the middle of the Paleogene period. Its remains, consisting of a lower second molar and a lower incisor, were recovered from the Bang Mark Pit at the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province.

According to recent reports, although only two teeth have been identified, they offer valuable clues about rodent gigantism, the evolutionary process through which rodents develop unusually large bodies. The discovery suggests that Southeast Asia played a more significant role in the early evolution of giant rodents than scientists had recognized.

Giant Rodents Have a Much Older History Than Expected.

"Today, the largest living rodent is the capybara, but very large rodents are not restricted to recent ecosystems," remarked Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and co-author of the study. "Giant rodents evolved repeatedly during the later history of the group, mostly in South America. This discovery suggests that Southeast Asia also played an crucial role in the early evolutionary history of large-bodied rodents.".

The newly identified animal's name reflects both its impressive size and its connection to Thailand. Yakamys combines "yak," the Thai word for giant, with "mys," the Greek word for mouse or rat.

The second part of its scientific name recognizes an crucial supporter of scientific research in Thailand.

"The species name, sirindhornae, honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her longstanding support for science and paleontological research in Thailand," Millien noted.

How Massive Was This 34-Million-Year-Old Rodent?

To estimate the animal's size, the research team applied seven established methods that use tooth measurements to calculate body mass. Their results suggest that Yakamys sirindhornae weighed approximately 30 kilograms, making it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including Hulgana.

That would have made the newly discovered species exceptionally large compared with its contemporaries. However, the researchers emphasize that determining an extinct animal's weight from a small number of fossilized teeth involves considerable uncertainty.

"This is only a ballpark figure, as there is substantial uncertainty associated with fossil body-mass estimation," Millien remarked.

The limited fossil evidence also makes it difficult to reconstruct how Yakamys evolved or what its life was like. Additional discoveries will be needed to better understand its physical characteristics, ecological role, and evolutionary relationships.

International Research Uncovers Thailand's Prehistoric Past.

The fossils were identified through an ongoing international collaboration investigating ancient mammals in Thailand's Krabi Basin. The project brings together scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations, including CNRS and Université de Poitiers.

In a recent development, by revealing evidence of an unusually large rodent in Southeast Asia 34 million years ago, the discovery expands scientists' understanding of where and when rodent gigantism emerged. Future fossil finds could help establish how these ancient giants lived and how their evolution relates to the enormous rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.

The research received support from CNRS, Université de Poitiers, Université de Montpellier, McGill University, and the Department of Mineral Resources of Thailand.

#154. Breaking: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (video, photos)

Breaking: 100 launches! Rocket Lab sends Earth-observing satellite to orbit on milestone mission (video, photos)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's Upcoming Zealand site on Saturday (Nov.
  • The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a major one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company.
  • Industry observers note that rocket Lab introduced for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-newly introduced Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocket Lab just hit the century mark.

Sources indicate that an Electron rocket topped with a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite lifted off from Rocket Lab's Upcoming Zealand site on Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT; 6:30 p.m. local New Zealand time).

The mission, which Rocket Lab called "The Mountain God Rises," was a major one: It marked the 100th launch to date for the California-based company.

Industry observers note that rocket Lab introduced for the first time in May 2017, sending the brand-newly introduced Electron up on a test flight from New Zealand. That effort failed, but Electron bounced back on its second-ever liftoff, delivering several cubesats to low Earth orbit (LEO) in January 2018.

In the years since, the 59-foot-tall (18 meters) Electron has become one of the most prolific and reliable rockets in the world, carrying small payloads to the final frontier for a variety of customers.

And it hit the century mark on Saturday in record-breaking fashion: No commercially developed rocket has gotten there faster, not even SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9, according to Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck.

According to recent reports, "It's an unprecedented milestone for a commercial small-lift orbital rocket, and a threshold rarely crossed in modern spaceflight," Beck noted on Monday (Nov. 9), during Rocket Lab's third-quarter earnings call with investors. "But what matters most to us and our customers is that we have achieved a 96% reliability rate across 99 debuts.".

Electron met the moment in style on Saturday morning, thanks to some fancy livery.

"Black rocket 🤝 Golden milestone. Electron is all dressed up for launch 100," Rocket Lab said via X on Tuesday (Nov. 10), in a post that shared a photo of the specially painted first stage.

Not all of Rocket Lab's missions have gone orbital, it should be noted: A suborbital variant of Electron known as HASTE, which customers use to test technologies in a hypersonic flight environment, has nine missions under its belt to date.

"The Mountain God Rises" was Rocket Lab's 11th launch to date for the Tokyo-based company iQPS, which is building a constellation of three dozen synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites in LEO. And all went to blueprint on the mission: Electron's upper "kick stage" deployed a single iQPS spacecraft 357 miles (575 kilometers) above Earth.

SAR satellites can see through cloud cover and image our planet at night as well as during the day, offering key advantages over spacecraft that are optimized to view in optical wavelengths.

#152. These ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Have Lost Their Dark Matter

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1633 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED

These ‘Ghostly’ Galaxies Have Lost Their Dark Matter

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • In a recent development, about 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right.
  • Sources indicate that dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

In a recent development, about 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.

Sources indicate that dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.

Recent findings suggest that but these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?

Industry observers note that A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three newly introduced galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.

It’s a convincing explanation for many experts—one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.

Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.

Recent findings suggest that these bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the latest study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark-matter-lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars—and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.

That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji noted.

Sources indicate that what, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s—and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin—cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.

In a recent development, “We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” noted Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”.

It has been revealed that dark matter, which makes up 27 percent of the universe—and 85 percent of all matter—interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.

It has been revealed that “You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” remarked Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding indicates no.”.

So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawaii to track the motions of those stars to estimate the galaxy's total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark-matter-deficient galaxy ever spotted.

In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists revealed that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.

That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.

Industry observers note that dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.

“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San Jose State University.

Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.

In a recent development, it’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.

Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.

Sources indicate that kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.

Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he stated. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.

“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.

It has been revealed that most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.

That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND states: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.

Industry observers note that MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull—for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances—the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.

Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the US-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of the universe—for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.

DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji stated.

According to recent reports, “I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson remarked. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”.

The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

#151. A massive latest simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1671 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

A massive latest simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.
  • Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide.
  • The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A powerful new computer simulation is allowing scientists to explore one of the most mysterious periods in cosmic history, when the universe emerged from darkness and the first stars and galaxies began to transform the cosmos.

Developed by researchers at MIT, Harvard University, and other institutions, the simulation, called Lumina, recreates the evolution of the early universe across a region roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide. It follows 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how galaxies formed, how radiation spread through space, and how the universe gradually became transparent to light.

The research, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), provides an unusually detailed picture of events that unfolded billions of years before our solar system existed.

How the Universe Entered Its Cosmic Dark Age.

The story begins with the Major Bang, when the universe existed in an extremely hot, dense state filled with electrons and other subatomic particles. This primordial plasma, described as initially smaller than a single atom, expanded rapidly and cooled as the universe grew.

Sources indicate that eventually, particles slowed enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, producing electrically neutral hydrogen. Around 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe entered a period known as the cosmic "dark age.".

In a recent development, although the universe had become transparent to much of the radiation left over from the Big Bang, stars had not yet formed to illuminate the cosmos. Neutral hydrogen filled space and could absorb certain types of radiation, including the ultraviolet light that would later emerge from the first stars.

Lumina allows researchers to investigate how this early environment evolved, eventually giving rise to the galaxies, stars, and other structures that helped bring the dark age to an end.

How the First Stars and Black Holes Transformed the Universe.

In a recent development, the simulation covers an immense region measuring 500 megaparsecs, equivalent to approximately 1.6 billion light-years. Within that volume, Lumina follows dark matter, gas, stars, and radiation (such as photons), capturing both the behavior of matter across enormous distances and the formation of individual galaxies.

One of its most key achievements is recreating two major changes in the early universe: hydrogen re-ionization and helium re-ionization.

Hydrogen re-ionization began as the first stars and galaxies produced increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation. This energetic light removed electrons from neutral hydrogen atoms, a process called "re-ionizing" the gas. As more hydrogen became ionized, the universe became increasingly transparent to ultraviolet light, allowing radiation to travel across much greater distances.

According to recent reports, this transformation helped clear the widespread neutral hydrogen that had dominated the early cosmos. Lumina reproduces the process in remarkable detail, showing how radiation from the first generations of stars gradually changed the conditions throughout space.

The simulation also follows helium re-ionization, which requires substantially more energetic radiation to strip electrons from helium.

It has been revealed that the results point to different sources driving these two transformations. Early stars and galaxies appear to have been primarily responsible for ionizing hydrogen, while actively feeding supermassive black holes supplied the intense radiation needed to ionize helium.

This is the first simulation to capture both processes together, offering a more complete view of how the early universe changed.

"Lumina does everything from small-scale star and galaxy formation to large-scale reionization of hydrogen and helium, in a volume that is 100 times larger than previous best simulations," says study author Mark Vogelsberger, a professor of physics at MIT.

The researchers are making Lumina available to other scientists, allowing its predictions about early cosmic structures to be compared with observations from existing and future telescopes. Such comparisons could help researchers better understand the events that shaped the first galaxies and stars.

Building a Virtual Universe With Half a Trillion Elements.

Lumina gets its name from the Latin word meaning "lights." Its underlying technology builds on IllustrisTNG, an earlier simulation developed by scientists at MIT and other institutions, including members of the Lumina research team.

IllustrisTNG models how galaxies form and evolve by following the interactions of dark matter, gas, and other physical processes from the Substantial Bang to the present day.

Industry observers note that to create Lumina, researchers upgraded the existing software so it could reproduce galaxy formation in comparable detail across a much larger region of space. They also incorporated a radiation transport model that calculates how light, including ultraviolet radiation, travels through the universe and interacts with surrounding matter.

Together, these improvements allow the simulation to track both the formation of galaxies and the enormous changes that radiation produces across cosmic distances.

Industry observers note that the resulting model contains approximately half a trillion individual elements, including particles of dark matter and cells representing gas. It provides roughly 30 times the resolution of IllustrisTNG while covering a region 100 times larger in volume than previous leading simulations.

It has been revealed that recreating billions of years of interactions across so many elements requires extraordinary computing resources. The researchers used Frontier, one of the world's most powerful supercomputers, located at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

"At peak scale, the calculation brings together the equivalent of more than 100,000 CPU cores and around 15,000 GPUs," says Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, an MIT co-author of the study. "Making all of those processors communicate efficiently while continuously evolving trillions of interacting pieces of information is itself an extraordinary feat of computer engineering.".

Watching the First Galaxies Emerge From Darkness.

Lumina begins approximately 45 million years after the Big Bang, during an era when neutral hydrogen dominated the universe.

Researchers initialized the simulation using conditions based on scientists' understanding of that period. They then allowed the model to calculate how gas and dark matter interacted throughout its half a trillion elements as cosmic time progressed.

At the same time, Lumina tracked how radiation appeared, spread, and interacted with matter, including the ultraviolet light produced by emerging stars.

The result is a virtual universe that scientists can explore at dramatically different scales, from the arrangement of matter across enormous cosmic distances down to the development of a single galaxy.

According to recent reports, on the project website, the researchers have released videos showing these processes in action. One offers a "zoom-in" from the entire simulated region to an individual disk-shaped galaxy. Another presents a time-lapse of the complete volume, showing how hydrogen re-ionization spreads across the universe over 2 billion years.

Recent findings suggest that "On the one hand, it's evolving dark matter as well as the gas in the universe, and on the other, it's also tracking how radiation travels," Zier explains. "We see dark matter and gas start to clump in these over-densities. And when we zoom in, we can see gas is falling into these dark matter haloes. Zooming in more, we see this is where the first galaxies form. And the first stars form in those first galaxies. Those stars then create radiation. The simulation then tracks that radiation, and we can zoom way out to see how that radiation travels out from stars, through the universe, until at some point it ionizes some neutral hydrogen.".

This ability to move between vastly different scales is one of Lumina's defining strengths. Researchers can examine the formation of individual galaxies while also observing how their combined radiation affects the universe on a much larger scale.

According to recent reports, "Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," Vogelsberger notes. "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation.".

A Newly introduced Way to Explore the Universe's Earliest History.

According to recent reports, the research team plans to use Lumina to investigate the large-scale arrangement of matter in the early universe. The simulation could also help predict the patterns of gravitational waves generated by ancient galaxies and black holes.

In a recent development, another major opportunity will come from comparing Lumina's virtual universe with real observations. Upcoming and upcoming telescopes are expected to collect increasingly detailed information about enormous numbers of distant galaxies, providing scientists with fresh ways to test their understanding of the early cosmos.

Because Lumina simulates such a large volume of space, it can generate extensive populations of galaxies that can be directly compared with these observations.

It has been revealed that "One of Lumina's major advantages is its sheer size," Shen states. "It produces enormous populations of simulated galaxies, finally allowing us to make comparisons with the very large galaxy samples that upcoming surveys will observe.".

By bringing together detailed galaxy formation, dark matter, gas, and the movement of radiation, Lumina offers researchers a powerful upcoming tool for reconstructing the universe's earliest chapters. It may help explain not only how the first galaxies took shape, but also how their stars and black holes transformed the surrounding cosmos.

According to recent reports, the study's MIT authors include Mark Vogelsberger, Xuejian (Jacob) Shen, and Teodora-Elena Bluichi. Other contributors include first author Oliver Zier (a former postdoc in the Vogelsberger Lab), Rongrong Liu, Sonja Koehler, and Lars Hernquist of the Harvard and Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics; Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas; Rahul Kannan of York University in Canada; and Volker Springel and Rüdiger Pakmor of the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics in Germany.

Recent findings suggest that the research received partial support from NASA and the National Science Foundation. It also used computing resources at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which is supported by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research programs within the Office of Science at the U.S. Department of Energy.

#148. Breaking: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1197 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

Breaking: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record.
  • According to recent reports, the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area.
  • Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

According to recent reports, the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade.

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

"The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," stated Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade.".

Although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman said.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss.

According to recent reports, ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

It has been revealed that A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

Sources indicate that in 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

"The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," noted Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.".

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole.

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

Sources indicate that to measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers rolled out instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations indicated that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

The Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Sources indicate that satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering.

Recent findings suggest that scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

Sources indicate that under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

These reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

Because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

The latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.

As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.

This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.

Industry observers note that “Tech bros were total nerds before," indicates Karen Clarkson, a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up. And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada.”.

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 1! (clockwise from top left): Giorgio Armani long-sleeved cashmere polo, $1,695; Lemaire workwear jacket, $1,050; The Row Nesper pant, $1,250; Giorgio Armani leather slippers, $1,850; Speciale cotton-mix stripe shirt; £295.

In a recent development, as a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ. Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”.

Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence notes is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”.

It has been revealed that if Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she claims. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed. I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”.

Jensen Huang’s Banished Biker Look 2! (clockwise from top left): The Row Vana jacket, $12,000; Speciale lambswool crew, £435; The Row Victor shirt, $1,290; Lemaire Rail Belt, $320; John Lobb City II New Standard shoes, $1,878; The Row Paulo corduroy pant, $1,590.

Let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue. “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi says. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”.

Industry observers note that clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.

“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson states. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It reveals he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”.

According to recent reports, jensen Huang's Banished Biker Look 3! (clockwise from top left): Paul Smith Ripstop field jacket, $1,025; Brunello Cucinelli alpaca-blend sweater, $3,400; The Row Sue pant, $2,300; Paul Smith Garson shoes, $475.

Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”.

It has been revealed that “There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” states Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”.

Giorgio Armani's Spring-Summer 2027 show in Milan.

However, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes. “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she states, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.

“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a fresh direction,” Clarkson says, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.

However, Clarkson states credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole fresh career.”.
