#60. Breaking: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1202 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

Breaking: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1202 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean.
  • Sources indicate that today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food.
  • A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dinosaurs living along ancient coastlines may have enjoyed an unexpected addition to their diets: seaweed and other food from the ocean. Latest research suggests that marine resources washed onto prehistoric beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey millions of years ago.

Sources indicate that today, powerful storms frequently deposit seaweed and other ocean material along shorelines, creating opportunities for animals that live on land to find additional food. Scientists call this process marine subsidization (MS). It is especially common in coastal environments and can become more notable when food on land is limited, such as during droughts.

A new study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution suggests that this relationship between land and sea existed during the age of dinosaurs. By examining chemical signatures preserved in fossils, researchers found evidence that ocean resources contributed to prehistoric food chains.

In a recent development, "We show that coastal terrestrial organisms in the greenhouse climates of the Cretaceous relied on marine resources to supplement their diets in a similar way that modern organisms do," said first author Dr. Clayton Forster, a geologist at the University of Arkansas. "We can identify that marine resources are passed along the food chain and incorporated in the minerals of bones and teeth of dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles, and fish.".

Mysterious Chemical Clues in Dinosaur Teeth.

The discovery helps explain a longstanding mystery involving the chemical composition of dinosaur teeth.

According to recent reports, plants contain two forms of carbon known as isotopes: 'light' (C-12) and 'heavy' (C-13). Scientists can measure the relative amounts of these isotopes, expressed as δ13C, to identify a chemical fingerprint that passes from food into the animals that consume it.

As animals eat, this carbon signature becomes incorporated into their tooth enamel. The δ13C value in enamel is typically higher than that of the food consumed, with living animals generally showing an increase of between 11 and 13 parts per thousand.

Industry observers note that however, previous measurements of dinosaur teeth have consistently revealed unusually high values. These readings also exceed what scientists would expect from animals that ate only plants growing on land, which generally have lower δ13C values than most marine plants.

One possible explanation is that dinosaurs, or the animals they consumed, were obtaining some of their nutrients from the ocean.

"By determining the carbon isotope composition of dinosaur, fish, and crocodile tooth enamel, we can determine what their primary dietary source was and if they were different between regions," explained Forster.

Fossils Reveal a Prehistoric Ocean Food Source.

To investigate, researchers examined fossils from (once) coastal locations bordering the Western Interior Seaway and the ancient coastline of the Gulf of Mexico. Around 100 million years ago, the Western Interior Seaway was an enormous inland sea that divided North America into two separate landmasses.

The team also analyzed fossils from locations farther inland, allowing them to compare animals that lived near the ocean with those that occupied landlocked environments.

The fossil deposits formed during two intervals of the Cretaceous Period: the early Albian (around 113-107 million years ago) and the early Cenomanian (approximately 100-96 million years ago).

Industry observers note that researchers used powdered fossil material to measure carbon isotope signatures from both periods. They also determined the latitudes where the animals had lived to investigate whether geography influenced the results.

Industry observers note that A clear pattern emerged. Fossils from coastal environments consistently contained higher δ13C values than those from the inland formation. Remarkably, the coastal signatures remained similar across different locations, regardless of latitude or geological age.

These findings provide the first evidence of marine subsidization in prehistoric ecosystems, indicating that nutrients originating in the ocean were entering food chains on land millions of years ago.

Seaweed May Have Been on the Dinosaur Menu.

The researchers next considered what ocean food source could explain the widespread chemical signatures.

"Coastal-dwelling organisms must have eaten some kind of organic matter from the ocean, or prey that had done so. This pattern is shared from fish to megaherbivores and indicates that the extra carbon source must have been low in the food-chain to affect both aquatic and terrestrial animals," Forster explained.

Recent findings suggest that for the same chemical pattern to appear in such a wide variety of animals, the marine food source would likely have entered the food chain near its base. It also needed to be something that existed along coastlines but was absent farther inland, while remaining available for millions of years.

Seaweed emerged as the most likely explanation.

"Few organisms meet these criteria besides marine macroalgae or macrophytes - seaweeds," said Forster. "Given the almost ubiquitous behavior of large coastal herbivores today to supplement their diet with seaweeds, it's likely that most of the sampled herbivorous dinosaurs were no different.".

According to recent reports, modern plant-eating animals living near coastlines often consume seaweed to supplement their diets. The fossil evidence suggests that many herbivorous dinosaurs may have behaved similarly, with marine nutrients also passing to other animals through the food chain.

Not Every Dinosaur Had a Taste for the Sea.

Despite the widespread evidence of marine nutrients in coastal food webs, the researchers found that not every dinosaur took advantage of these resources.

One notable exception was Tenontosaurus tilletti, a large plant-eating dinosaur whose fossils have been discovered at numerous locations dating to the Cretaceous Period.

According to recent reports, its tooth enamel contained δ13C values comparable to those of modern animals that feed on plants growing on land. This suggests that Tenontosaurus tilletti did not rely on marine food sources, even though other dinosaurs apparently did.

In a recent development, the difference also strengthens the researchers' interpretation of the fossil evidence. If geological processes occurring after death had altered the carbon signatures in dinosaur teeth, the same unusual values would be expected more broadly. Instead, the variation between species suggests that the elevated readings reflect genuine differences in diet.

An Ancient Connection Between Land and Ocean.

Although the findings provide strong evidence that marine resources supported the coastal ecosystems examined, vital questions remain.

The available fossils do not include specimens from polar or equatorial regions during the early Albian and early Cenomanian. As a result, scientists cannot yet determine how widespread this feeding behavior was across different latitudes.

Additional studies will also be needed to establish whether similar relationships existed during other geological periods, including the earlier Jurassic Period and the later early Cenozoic Era.

Beyond revealing a surprising possibility about what dinosaurs ate, the discovery highlights how closely life on land has been connected to the ocean throughout Earth's history.

"Our study emphasizes the connections between terrestrial and marine ecosystems," concluded Forster. "They are deeply intertwined and have been for hundreds of millions of years. It highlights the importance of environmental linkages across time and space and protecting them where they exist today.".

NASA Armstrong Public Affairs Specialist.

In a recent development, as a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time.

In a recent development, endeavour’s newly introduced home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers.

According to recent reports, “Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” noted Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.”.

Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images.

According to recent reports, “The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” noted Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.”.

Photographer Carla Thomas stated seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight.

According to recent reports, endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to strategy the shots,” Thomas noted. “I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters. We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles. Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these challenges in the planning process.”.

The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier.

Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions. The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that watchOS 27 introduces a solid set of upgrades to your wrist—assuming your Apple Watch supports it. While the newest enhancement isn't Apple's most feature-filled, it does include a number of changes that improve the way you exercise, track your health, and locate missing items. That's especially true for anyone with the latest Series 12 or Ultra 4. If your Apple Watch supports watchOS 27, you should know about these 10 hacks:.

With watchOS 27, Apple changed what double-pressing the Digital Crown does. Instead of opening the app switcher, it now triggers Audio Intelligence—if you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. If you don't have access to those features, the gesture now does nothing.

It seems Apple realized the mistake, however, as evidenced by watchOS 27.2. When you're using an app while running this latest upgrade, press and hold the bottom part of the watch's screen, and you'll trigger the app switcher. You can now jump to a different app, or close an app that isn't working. Sadly, this only works when you're already in an app, and not when you're on the Home Screen, but it's certainly better than nothing.

While you can load up multiple complications on your Apple Watch, they aren't exactly dynamic. That's why I'm a big fan of the Smart Stack widgets on the Apple Watch, which enhancement dynamically to show contextual information. Now, with the newly introduced Siri Modular Face, you can access dynamic widgets on the Home Screen. If you've just parked your car, for example, you'll see a widget showing its location; likewise, if you have an upcoming calendar appointment, it will be front and center.

To use the Siri Modular watch face, tap and hold on the screen, go to the end of the list, tap the Plus button, and find and add the Siri Modular watch face. Once you do, you'll start seeing dynamic widgets when you wake up your watch. Don't expect much personalization from this watch face, however. You can customize the colors and add three small complications, but that's it.

According to recent reports, the double-tap gesture is one of my favorite Apple Watch features. By tapping your thumb and index finger together twice, you can do things like answer a call or reply to a message. In watchOS 27, Apple took the gesture one step forward. You can now use the double-tap gesture to scroll through your widgets; if you perform a single tap, it then opens the highlighted widget or the shortcut. This means you can open and browse the weather app, or start a workout, without ever touching your Apple Watch's screen.

Industry observers note that your Apple Watch's new Music Recognition app has native Shazam integration. What's more, Shazam will record your request even when you're offline and away from your iPhone. The moment you reconnect, the service will identify the songs, which you can see in the Shazam app on your iPhone or Apple Watch.

In a recent development, it seems like Apple has a library of songs it uses for offline recognition, because in my testing, it was able to recognize a Coldplay song instantly, even when in Airplane mode. To use it, you can either open the Music Recognition app, or you can add the widget for faster access. Scroll up on the Home Screen, go to the bottom of the screen, tap the Edit button, then the Plus button, and add the Music Recognition widget.

It has been revealed that apple Watches have traditionally lacked a live step count widget or complication. To find your step count, you had to go to the bottom of the Activity app, or rely on third-party apps. But even still, these apps never showed live data. You’d always have to wait a couple of seconds to see the updated stats.

According to recent reports, now, if you own the latest Apple Watch Series 12 or the Ultra 4, you can add a live step count widget or complication to the Apple Watch face or the Smart Stack. This will show you your precise step count at all times. To use it, go to the bottom of the Smart Stack, tap the Edit button, then tap the Plus button. Here, find and add the latest Step count widget.

According to recent reports, siri is no longer a voice assistant that you use for one-off tasks. With Siri AI, you can now carry on multiple conversations with context and memory. It's not as robust as ChatGPT or Claude, but you can use Siri AI for brainstorming, researching, and jotting down ideas for later.

The Siri AI app on the iPhone highlights all your conversations, and so does the Apple Watch. This means you can continue your Siri AI conversations and view past chats on your Apple Watch. To use it, press the Digital Crown once, then tap the Siri app icon in the center. This will open up all your conversations instead of calling upon Siri. Tap a conversation to continue your chat on the Apple Watch. Of course, anything you do here will be reflected in the Siri app on your iPhone.

Sources indicate that the latest Find My app on the Apple Watch demonstrates a single map for finding people, devices, and items. This means you can now locate your family members who are sharing their location with you, as well as AirTags or other Find My items from the watchOS app.

After opening the app, you can use the Digital Crown to zoom in or out of the map. Use touch to pan around. The map doesn't show all items and people at once, though. Tap the Menu button at the bottom-right corner, and then switch between People, Items, or Devices. If you have multiple items, you can scroll through them using the Digital Crown.

It has been revealed that while it's not a Whoop-level feature, the Apple Watch now includes a Readiness score. Instead of individually looking at your training load, sleep score, and vitals, you now have one number that gives you the whole picture.

Recent findings suggest that the Readiness score ranges from 0 to 10 and is based on your recent fitness activity, sleep data, and background health monitoring. If you have a score of 8 to 10, your Apple Watch thinks you can push yourself, or "go for it," as it says; if it's below 5, the watch thinks you should consider lighter activity. This feature, though, is only available on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. You can use the new Readiness app on your Apple Watch to see this data, but you can also access it on your iPhone in the Fitness app's new Readiness section.

It has been revealed that low Power Mode isn't your only option when it comes to extending the battery life for your Apple Watch. watchOS 27 offers a special Max Extended Workout mode just for long workouts. With it, your Apple Watch disables some features, like splits and alerts, and reduces the frequency of GPS and heart rate readings, in the hopes of extending your battery throughout your entire exercise. To use it, go to the Workout app and select the workout you want. Tap the Goals button in the top-right corner, and choose the Extended option. Then, switch to the Max Extended option and start your workout.

Industry observers note that the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come with a set of Audio Intelligence features that use the microphones on the Apple Watch, paired with AI models (both local and cloud-based), to identify sounds, music, and record conversation. Thanks to this latest feature, one of the iPhone's accessibility features also makes its way to the Apple Watch.

Sources indicate that sound Recognition can alert you when it hears sirens, alarms, doorbells, and more, even when your iPhone isn’t around. To set this up, go to the Settings app on your iPhone and navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here, enable the sounds you want to monitor, and make sure to turn on the Detect using Apple Watch toggle.

#57. Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (959 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space

Why hasn't the 'Blaze Star' exploded yet? Astronomers weigh in on what to expect

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "fresh" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion.
  • Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant.
  • Recent findings suggest that "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "fresh" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out.

Industry observers note that T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold. Next comes a dramatic nova explosion that causes the star to flare to 1,000 times its usual brightness before gradually settling down and repeating the cycle.

Recent findings suggest that "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon," Bradley Schaefer of the Louisiana State University Department of Physics and Astronomy told Space.com in an email. "Everyone is very confident on this. But we cannot make high-accuracy measures of the rate of gas falling onto the surface of the white dwarf, and we do not have a high accuracy measure of the trigger mass for the substantial hydrogen bomb." Schaefer continued.

Sources indicate that historical observations reveal that the last nova eruption reached Earth in 1946, which places us well inside the window for another dramatic brightening of T. CrBb. However, the unpredictability of the white dwarf's feeding makes it difficult to pin down exactly when the explosion will become visible from Earth.

Industry observers note that "The exact date of the upcoming T CrB eruption depends primarily on how fast the gas coming from its companion star is accumulating on the surface of the white dwarf," explained Schaefer. "When some specific trigger mass has accumulated, then T CrB will erupt. For the last 80 years, we have been watching the gas pile up on the white dwarf surface, and we know that it must be near the trigger threshold.".

Astronomers have tried to predict T CrB's brightening by comparing a recent fluctuation in the light of the distant star system to a similar event that occurred in the runup to the 1946 event.

In a recent development, "There have already been some dimming and brightening episodes that caused excitement but did not yet turn into the main event," Elizabeth Hays, lab chief at NASA's Astroparticle Physics Laboratory at the Goddard Spaceflight Center, told Space.com in an email. "It is likely that the nova will happen in the next few years but we still don't know exactly when. I can't give you a guaranteed prediction, but I will be a little surprised if it gets to 2030, or 84 years past the last eruption.".

Recent findings suggest that hays notes that the intense light from the red giant dramatically outshines the dimmer white dwarf, making detailed observation challenging. There is also no way to precisely measure the temperature and pressure of the matter lurking near the surface of the smaller star. "Predicting nova explosions are a little like predicting the weather; conditions may be right but the timing of the storm can be uncertain.".

There'll be no visual warning of the eruption before it reaches Earth, though according to Hays there could be an early flash of light in the X-ray spectrum.

"The world's amateur astronomers have been doing an awesome job of keeping T CrB under hair-trigger monitoring roughly every minute or two, so when T CrB has brightened by around one magnitude, then alerts will spread around the world within minutes," remarked Schaefer.

Industry observers note that once the call goes out, telescopes and observatories around the world will kick into gear, running pre-prepared observation programmes to capitalize on the rare and cataclysmic event. "When the nuclear runaway process starts, it will take off and peak very rapidly, in less than a day.".

The nova will see the star jump from its normal brightness of magnitude +10 — which is beyond the detection limit of the naked eye — to magnitude +1.7, making it appear as if a star brighter than the North Star Polaris has suddenly burst to life in the night sky.

"The brightness will fall below naked-eye visibility in dark places within a couple of days and become too faint for binoculars within about a week," stated Hays. "Outside the visible band, for example, in radio, X-ray and gamma rays, light caused by the eruption will be visible for months or even years. ".

T CrB can be found glowing close to the magnitude +4.28 star Epsilon Coronae Borealis in the constellation Corona Borealis during the early evening in November, with the constellations of Hercules and Bootes on either side.

It will dip below the horizon for viewers in the U.S. just a few hours after sunset, before re-emerging into the northeastern sky in the predawn hours.

Want to capture a photo of T. CrB when it erupts? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the night sky, along with our picks of the best cameras, lenses and smart telescopes that are perfect for capturing the majesty of the starry realm.

#54. Industry News: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1305 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily

Industry News: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed.
  • In a recent development, quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos.
  • Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

In a recent development, quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

Astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

It has been revealed that rolled out in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," claims Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so rapidly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics.".

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars.

Recent findings suggest that until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

Recent findings suggest that "Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting.".

Sources indicate that among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn.

Recent findings suggest that two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

According to recent reports, these discoveries establish latest records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," notes Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

"The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a major step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level.".

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies.

Recent findings suggest that one of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Sources indicate that their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where latest stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an notable glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

It has been revealed that these quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

According to recent reports, "Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," indicates ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants.

It has been revealed that euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

Recent findings suggest that "Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground.".

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide newly introduced clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

#52. NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
  • Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object.
  • The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Recent findings suggest that astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.

It has been revealed that hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble's high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.

By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.

Industry observers note that the unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

According to recent reports, panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I reveals a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.

It has been revealed that some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.

According to recent reports, most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.

But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.

Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.

In a recent development, these strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

#51. Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)

Skeleton found in Denmark came from man who witnessed the arrival of farming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Newscientist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.
  • “What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a upcoming group of people?” says Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.
  • A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Analysis of a skeleton from Denmark, nicknamed “Rødhals Man”, hints that the individual lived through one of the most fundamental changes in human history: the transition from hunter-gathering to farming.

“What was it like to live through such a momentous transition, seeing the archipelago where your ancestors had fished being transformed by the arrival of a upcoming group of people?” says Anders Fischer at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden.

A lost ancient script reveals how writing as we know it really began.

Rødhals Man lived some 6000 years ago, and was discovered on the small island of Sejerø in Denmark in the 1950s, buried in a shell midden – an ancient accumulation of discarded sea shells and other domestic refuse. Previous investigations have indicated he was unusual. He lived some time between about 3800 and 3900 BC, near the start of the Neolithic period in the area, when diets changed to consist predominantly of terrestrial food produced by farmers. And yet Rødhals Man, with his genetic ancestry typical of the local Mesolithic Ertebølle culture of hunter-gatherers, didn’t seem to have eaten that diet: a study in 1981 indicated that he ate mainly seafood.

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something crucial,” says Fischer.

In a recent development, to get a better idea of what was going on, Fischer and his colleagues have now looked at the levels of rare isotopes of elements including carbon, nitrogen and sulphur in several of the man’s bones, which renewed at different rates during his life, preserving different snapshots in time. The researchers also analysed the chemical signatures in one of his teeth, which preserve a record of diet from childhood. Collectively, the data gave the team an opportunity to look for clues about how Rødhals Man’s diet changed over the 30 to 40 years of his life.

“You can see that most of the time, the primary food source is what we call the eelgrass biotype. This is not eelgrass itself, but the animals that live in the thick forests of this sea grass in shallow water,” states team member John Meadows at Kiel University in Germany. This could have been animals like molluscs, flatfish or eels, he says.

But from the age of about 11 onwards, Rødhals Man’s diet became unlike that of any Mesolithic hunter-gatherer recorded so far, with increasing amounts of terrestrial, probably farmed, protein.

Rødhals Man’s burial also shares more similarities with burials of Early Neolithic farmers than those of Late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, because his bones lacked an added coating of ochre staining and his grave featured a stone frame.

The evidence leads Meadows to suggest that Rødhals Man interacted with the Neolithic farmers and adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his ancestors on the small island. Sejerø is just 12 square kilometres in area, but is only about 5 kilometres from Zealand, which is around 7000 square kilometres.

An analysis of ancient genomes has revealed that the descendants of Stone Age farmers in Europe and hunter-gatherers gained more genes from the latter group than expected.

It has been revealed that “He was on a tiny island with very little in the way of wild terrestrial resources to live on,” notes Meadows. “He may have spent part of the year living in a farming community on Zealand and part living on the island and only eating fish.”.

In a recent development, “It is quite amazing that all this information could be retrieved from one single skeleton,” says Mathias Currat at the University of Geneva. “I think this is an interesting story, which probably represents part of the main story in this area.”.

It would be unusual to change diet in this way, says Marcello Mannino at Aarhus University in Denmark. “Such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”.

He says it is likely that the Neolithic farmers probably first occupied areas where soil conditions were better, such as in central Zealand, and were slower to inhabit more marginal areas. “We need to find more human remains that span the transition to try to understand how it happened,” he says.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.

Industry observers note that long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.

Recent findings suggest that the Yeti 2's biggest upgrades stares you directly in the face after taking it out of the box. The built-in screen and dial allow for on-the-fly adjustments right on the microphone. No software required. While I was a skeptic at first, I quickly found this little screen to be significantly more convenient than the alternative. It can be used to adjust gain, enable different post-processing settings, and configure the sound profile of the microphone.

More importantly, the screen can promptly provide insights into audio quality at a glance. The main screen reveals a graph of the gain-adjusted input volume, which is what the microphone is sending to your computer. It can also display a histogram of volume over time, a pattern to show what direction input is coming from, or … a pixel-art Yeti. This little guy looks confused when you’re quiet, happy when you’re talking at a normal volume, and alarmed when you’re too loud for the microphone to handle. Within the G Hub app, the icons can be swapped out with any of Logi’s other premade avatars (a dragon, flower, frog, or jellyfish), or freely customized with your own images using a simple drag-and-drop menu. This is the least functional feature of the microphone, but it’s an endearing and intuitive way to indicate audio quality at a glance.

It has been revealed that the screen also has quite a few adjustable menus for different features, including a de-noise function with four levels, five EQ presets, a pattern customizer with eight default options, and a multitude of toggleable settings to clean up and improve recording quality. While the settings can’t be customized using the screen, the G Hub application provides more in-depth adjustments for how intense each of these settings are, along with explanations of how they work and when to use them.

Industry observers note that the microphone comes with a basic desk-mounted stand in the box, which uses two rubber grommets and a felt panel underneath to isolate it from the desk. While I was initially worried about this picking up resonance from typing, the isolation mount and noise cancellation settings manage to make it sound normal even when placed directly next to a keyboard.

Industry observers note that hanging the microphone from a boom arm definitely doesn’t feel as natural as the stand, but it is entirely possible with the threaded hole on the underside. The headphone jack’s placement on top is inconvenient, and the microphone feels incredibly long when hanging from above. The screen’s display can be flipped 180 degrees, though this means the adjustment knob is now on top of the screen. When using the knob, your hand will likely be in the way of both the display and the proximity sensor, which can be a bit annoying. The microphone is designed to be used with the included stand, but it’s still entirely usable with an arm as well.

In a recent development, the most impressive part of this microphone was how little I had to do when using it, since the automatic settings are so dialed-in. During my entire time with the microphone, I didn’t need to adjust the gain at all. Outside of specifically testing functionality, I didn’t even have any reason to open the Logitech G Hub app. All of the vital settings are able manage themselves entirely from the microphone itself.

The automatic gain control on the microphone is fantastic and requires basically no input outside of very fringe instances. The system has a proximity sensor to determine your distance from the microphone, which it then uses to determine the input range and angle. At essentially any distance, I found the microphone to pick up my voice and normalize it to an acceptable volume, albeit with some audio quality degradation at longer distances. Namely, there are some problems with echoing and loss of midrange frequencies, resulting in a more hollow sound overall. But the loss is fairly limited.

Similarly, the noise reduction works fantastically. The de-noiser has four levels total, ranging from “none” to “maximum.” The higher the de-noiser setting is cranked up, the more muted and claustrophobic sound. With the setting at maximum, I was able to place the microphone behind my mechanical keyboard (which is all-aluminum with no foam, meaning it’s LOUD) with zero interference or noise, as opposed to setting the microphone between myself and my keyboard. On the other hand, at lower levels, the microphone was able to completely drown out a quieter keyboard or farther-away background noise with no issues. That's seriously impressive.

Much like the original Yeti, the follow-up uses a cluster of three directional capsules, with the different settings adjusting the relative sensitivity of each. The directional functionality can swap between standard front-facing sensitivity with three degrees (standard, focused, and hyper-focused), 360-degree pickup, and an “interview” mode that listens on either side of the microphone. There’s also an option for Stereo mode, which separates the left and right levels from the front. However, I found that this mode struggled to pick up louder or higher-pitched directional noises, with claps or snaps registering on both sides equally. This is not a huge matter, but ASMR fans beware.

Opening up the microphone, it appears that two of the clusters are facing towards the user at 45-degree angles, while the third is facing away from them. This explains why the stereo mode only works for the half of the microphone facing the user and doesn’t have 360-degree coverage. Besides this, the construction of the microphone is incredibly simple, and the entire microphone can be disassembled in a few easy steps.

Industry observers note that comparing to the original model, the Yeti 2 has vastly more built-in tools to actively process and refine audio. The core microphones sound incredibly similar though—even down to the default sound profiles, which highlight the midrange and create an overall “warm” sound. The sound profile can be tweaked to some degree using the built-in equalizer. I did notice that the Yeti 2 has a slightly less bass-y sound during use though.

Every sample I recorded during testing sounded crisp and clear, though I had one consistent complaint. Even without any of the processing sounds enabled, there was still a tiny bit of noise that wasn't present in other microphones. After experimenting with EQ and settings, it seems this is an inherent part of the microphone’s sound profile. While the Yeti 2 can produce a more clean immediate output with all of its built-in features and processing, it won’t have the same potential for audio quality as some other high-quality microphones.

It has been revealed that ultimately, with its processing, this microphone is going to be ideal for any kind of live interactions or broadcasts. This means livestreams, video calls, and in-game chat will be its bread-and-butter. Similarly, it will be great for someone who doesn’t have the patience and/or technical know-how to edit audio. But if you’re a professional who knows how to do those things, it really doesn’t make sense to choose this microphone over something with a higher ceiling for audio quality, especially since you’re limited to USB-C input instead of having an option for XLR.

Sources indicate that the most impressive part of this microphone is the price. A standard Yeti—which is old enough to still use a Mini-USB connection—is $140 from Logitech. Meanwhile, the Yeti 2 is $160. The breadth features gained for $20 is absolutely mind-boggling and makes it an obvious choice for most microphone buyers. It should be noted that the original Yeti is often discounted to as low as $110, which might make the decision between the two a bit more difficult if you're on a budget.

According to recent reports, personally, I will always prefer an audio setup that doesn’t try to merge everything into one device. My current setup is a separate microphone and DAC, and the ability to customize, replace, and even just physically move around individual components outweighs the convenience of an all-in-one setup. That allows me to fine-tune my setup to exactly how I want to sound. But if you those who want a simple, plug-and-play solution for a fraction of the price, it’s really hard to argue with the Yeti 2.

I Analyzed the Seven Biggest AI Chatbots to Determine How Safe They Are for Kids

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications.
  • It has been revealed that the major AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe.
  • Recent findings suggest that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI safety for both adults and children is under greater scrutiny than ever before, with a growing number of questions and concerns appearing around how beneficial or otherwise these conversational bots actually are for our mental well-being—even without considering their energy use, ethics, or economic implications. At the same time, an increasing number of apps and services are becoming age-gated in a growing number of countries around the world, as governments realize that letting kids loose on AI apps, social media platforms, and the web at large might not be the best idea for their ongoing development and prosperity.

It has been revealed that the major AI apps, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are right in the center of these trends, and the companies behind them are taking steps that they promise will keep children safe. If you want to know what youngsters in your family may be getting exposed to, and what you can do about it, here's the rundown.

Recent findings suggest that openAI's ChatGPT has one of the more comprehensive setups in terms of parental controls. The minimum age for users is 13, and if you're under 18, you need to have parental consent to open an account—age is predicted via several signals, including what times of day you use ChatGPT and what you talk about.

Accounts for under-18s automatically become ChatGPT for Teens accounts. There's more of a focus on learning and study (with a dedicated study mode), as well as "age-appropriate safeguards to help reduce exposure to sensitive or potentially harmful content." There are built-in protections for "harmful topics," including sexual, romantic, or violent roleplay, graphic violence, and self-harm. These work on top of the safeguards for all owners that limit chats about physical harm and illegal activity.

These ChatGPT for Teens accounts can also be linked to a parental account—but while parental consent is required for under-18s to use the service, ChatGPT clearly claims that teens do have the option to break the link if they want. If you do persuade your kid to keep your accounts connected, you can set time limits on when the AI bot can be used, and tweak some of the sensitivity settings. However, you can't view any conversations.

To set up parental controls from ChatGPT on the web, click your profile icon (bottom left), then Settings > Parental controls > Add family member and follow the instructions. It's also worth bearing in mind that ChatGPT app can also be used for free, anonymously, in any web browser, though OpenAI says consumers accessing the AI this way are subject to the default under-18s limits (and can't save chats or access an archive).

Recent findings suggest that gemini is tied into everything else Google does, and follows the broader rules for Google accounts: No under-13s, unless you're part of a family group and using an account managed by an adult. You can manage your family through the Family Link portal on the web, though as far as parental controls specific to Gemini go, you can only enable or disable access to the AI (settings like screen time apply across all enabled apps).

It has been revealed that for all under-18s (partly identified through age estimation), whether or not they're part of a managed family group, Google applies some additional protections. They include preventing the AI from taking on a persona, guarding against emotional dependence on the AI, and discouraging bullying and other forms of harassment. There are also safeguards to limit chats about age-restricted substances like alcohol or vapes, and mental health issues like eating disorders.

These protections for minors are applied in addition to the usual guardrails in Gemini for everyone. The guardrails should lead you away from conversations about self-harm, suicide, violence, and illegal activities, and offer quick links to support in times of crisis. However, Google itself admits that these filters aren't perfect.

As with ChatGPT, there's a loophole of sorts in that anyone can start chatting with Gemini, for free inside a web browser, with no checks at all. These conversations can't be saved and come up against usage limits fairly swiftly, but they're only protected by the general restrictions for all accounts, not the ones specific to minors.

Industry observers note that meta AI will show up in several apps that young people and children are likely to use, including WhatsApp and Instagram, as well as having its own separate app on the web and on phones. The standard restrictions for Meta's social media accounts apply to its AI too: A minimum age of 13, and restrictions for all under-18s. Like many other platforms, it uses some AI magic to flag up accounts being used by minors.

Sources indicate that if you're under 18 and on a Meta Teen account, you'll come up against blocks if you try to get Meta AI to engage in sexual or romantic roleplay, or discuss alcohol or substance misuse. Chats on topics such as eating disorders and self-harm will prompt the AI to offer guidance towards relevant support services.

According to recent reports, meta offers a comprehensive parental control setup for its apps, including Meta AI, but connecting a parent account isn't compulsory for teens. This is handled through the Meta Family Center portal, and parents can get reports on the general topics that kids are chatting about with AI—though they don't get the exact transcripts or prompts. Any self-harm or suicide discussion can trigger an alert to the connected parent account.

All owners, under 18 or over 18, get support and crisis intervention responses when chatting about suicide and self-harm, and there are strict limits on discussing illegal and harmful acts, including drug use and cyberbullying, as well as sexual and adult content.

Industry observers note that apple customers have to be 13 or over to have an account, which is required to access Siri AI—anyone younger needs to have an account created for them by an adult, and these accounts can only get at the basic, older Siri. Date of birth must be declared when opening an Apple account, with tighter checks rolling out in many parts of the world.

Recent findings suggest that anyone over the age of 13 can have an Apple account and use the Siri AI app, with or without a connected parent account, as it stands in most U.S. states. This means the well-being safeguards are essentially the same for teens as they are for adults: There are safeguards around self-harm, suicide, sexual and violent content, and illegal commands. It's one of the more conservative AIs when it comes to what it will talk about.

Recent findings suggest that the new and improved Siri AI can be managed to some extent by the new parental controls available in iOS 27 and Apple's other software updates for 2026—Apple has clearly seen the way the wind is blowing—but this is optional for teens. It depends on whether or not you can corral your kids into a Family Sharing group.

Sources indicate that if your teens are in your family group of consumers, then the standard Screen Time rules apply for controlling app usage limits and device access (in iOS Settings, tap your name, then Family to get at them). There are also options for disabling certain Siri AI features, such as the writing tools or the image creation capabilities.

It has been revealed that like Gemini/Google and Apple/Siri, Copilot is tied into the wider Microsoft ecosystem, and access for under-18s can be managed through it. Owners must be 13 or older to hold a Microsoft or a Copilot account—and again, there's some underlying tech in place to detect anyone who might be deliberately lying about their age.

If you've got a teen using Copilot, you can manage their access through the standard Microsoft Family Safety portal. You're able to enable or disable Copilot access, set times during which Copilot can and can't be used, and disable certain features like image generation or voice mode. Parents can't read the Copilot chats of their kids, though.

Parental supervision is optional—a teen aged 13–17 can use Copilot without linking their account to an adult one. Microsoft claims customers identified as under 18 won't see personalized results or ads, and will get age-appropriate responses regarding risky or harmful content, though there's not much detail on what that entails.

Industry observers note that more generally, content around self-harm, violence, adult content, harassment, and harmful or illegal activity is banned on the AI platform. Any prompts about suicide or drugs will bring up support options rather than answers, whether you're an adult or a young person using the service.

Ultimately that means that minors have the same access to Grok as adults, if they want it—an AI platform that combines "weak safety guardrails" and "a range of extremely harmful content" that includes "explicit sexual content, mental health risks, violent content, and inappropriate responses to... offensive content" (that's the Common Sense Media Report again).

Yes, this is the AI chatbot that has previously had a problem with deepfake porn imagery, and which has traditionally taken a rather casual attitude towards safety concerns, led by SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk. While illegal and harmful content is supposedly banned from Grok, its own FAQs admit that certain chats can result in "dialogue that may involve coarse language, crude humor, sexual situations, or violence.".

There is actually a Grok Kids Mode that limits the kind of content that can be shown and the conversation topics that can be added, but it requires users to self-declare themselves as minors and is easy to bypass. The advice from Common Sense Media seems to be the way to go with Grok: Do not let your teens access it.

Recent findings suggest that claude's approach to child safety is straightforward: You can only register for an account if you're over 18. It is possible to lie about your age when signing up, but like the other platforms, Anthropic looks at various "signals" in behavior to spot minors—if your account gets flagged, you have to verify your age using an option like face age estimation or Yoti.

There's no free web access to the chatbot, like there is with ChatGPT and Gemini, so if you're under 18, you're locked out from the service unless you know the behavioral tricks to get past Claude's detection systems.

Recent findings suggest that in terms of more general well-being protections on Claude, any chat around self-harm or suicide will guide people towards helplines and other resources for support. Conversations about illegal activities, disallowed speech, and explicit sexual content are banned from the platform. In recent months, Anthropic states it's also reduced AI sycophancy.

Sources indicate that that's something of a whistle-stop tour of the big seven AI chatbots, but if you're a parent, it should give you some idea of what's out there and how easy it is to access. Besides the parental controls built into these AIs (or not), you also have the settings available at the platform level—Android, iOS, Windows, macOS—to restrict the use of any potentially harmful apps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “The Amiga was my first school.” For pixel artist Klas Benjaminsson, that’s less nostalgia than a CV. The Swedish creator of the Masters of Pixel Art book series learned his craft on Commodore’s 16-bit wonder, and three decades later, he’s gone back to class, creating a brand-fresh artwork entirely on an original Amiga 1200 (the Amiga ranks in our best retro consoles guide).

Industry observers note that the result is Beyond the Screen: wildlife, lush vegetation and ocean life bursting out of a glowing monitor. It’s built from just 640 x 512 pixels and 32 colours, a canvas that would make a modern phone wallpaper blush. Benjaminsson first sketched in pencil, then brought it to life in Deluxe Paint 4. He calls the Amiga’s limits a “sweet spot”: tight enough to push against, generous enough to make something great.

It’s also a nod to Jim Sachs’ Amiga Lagoon, the picture that showed a generation what these machines could do, and a love letter to an era when your imagination really was the only limit.

In a recent development, the timing is no accident. Retro Games’ full-size Amiga 1200 replica, THEA1200, lands on 4 December. Unlike the A500 Mini we reviewed in 2022, it comes with a working keyboard and Workbench desktop, so it’s built for creating as well as playing.

According to recent reports, artists can join in too, with PosterSpy inviting its community to reimagine Benjaminsson’s piece in their own style. Need a pixel fix first? Dive into our 31 amazing pixel art examples or learn how to break into pixel art. Then read on as Benjaminsson explains why limits still make for better art, and which retro tools you should try first.

The new THEA1200 arrives on 4 December. See more of Klas Benjaminsson's poster art at PosterSpy x THEA1200.

Klas Benjaminsson: One key point in the initiative of THEA1200 is to recreate the Amiga 1200 in modern shape, so it made sense to honor the original platform.

KB: To be honest, the work "Amiga Lagoon" by Jim Sachs was a very notable piece from the beginning. It visualised the power and creativity of the Amiga, and we agreed that an indirect homage to this masterpiece would be suitable for this occasion.There was an idea to create a “flow” coming out from the screen, showing waves of animals, nature and wildlife - flowing and growing out from this creative computer. I wanted a feeling that communicated “only your imagination sets the limits”.From sketch to finish, animals changed and shifted positions. But I felt the core idea was good and continued the work until the end.

KB: For me personally, growing up with the Amiga 500 and 1200 graphic standards, these limitations became something of a sweet spot for me. Limited enough to make it interesting to push the borders on what could be done, but also good enough to make it possible to create some great designs.

According to recent reports, KB: Deluxe Paint 4 on the Amiga was where bulk of work was done. Photoshop and GrafX2 on the PC: importing the sketches and converting formats for export.

According to recent reports, KB: To be honest I think many of modern pixel artists are doing a great job. There are hundreds of active pixel artists right now, posting pixel art on a daily basis with no direct platform or set rules for limits in their work space, but they still set a limited palette and a certain pixel area for their work. I think it's an awesome homage to the old platforms, which lives on so vividly in these modern pixel art works even today.

KB: Digital graphics had a substantial impact in my youth. As a kid I enjoyed playing video games, but as a young aspiring “artist” I also studied the graphics of the many games I tried (both Arcade and on my own C64). It took several years until a friend of mine revealed me his brand fresh Amiga 500 with Deluxe Paint – that was the moment I realised I might be able to create something like that myself.I took the first steps on a very long and interesting journey on finally becoming an art director. The Amiga was my first school that defined much of my professional life.

Industry observers note that KB: There are many techniques that more or less could be described as artistic knowledge, which I learned on the Amiga but aren't unique for this medium/platform. But there are some routines that could be blamed on my background with old-school pixel art:- The importance of setting a palette early on in the design process.- To keep full control of the pixels and resolution.

Industry observers note that KB: The Amiga provides an interesting set of limitations to work with if you are into pixel art. Enforcing a specific resolution and a limited colour palette when creating pixel art is a very challenging and demanding practice, which forces the artist to be precise. With these clear restrictions in place, much more focus can be aimed at the actual creative work instead.

KB: I personally find it fascinating to take photos with a classic analogue camera, and see how the film can change with exposure settings. It's a special and rewarding experience to go through the processes by hand. You try and learn by mistakes, testing ideas, creating and discarding concepts, and finally finding a way to express your ideas. Digital tools can be a great help, working alongside you when sketching and trying out ideas. But there is a certain magic about when doing it by yourself, learning the craft.

It has been revealed that KB: If you are into pixel art, don't hesitate to try out Deluxe Paint or Brilliance! These are the original software from which most modern pixel art tools has taken their UI concepts, as well as the early versions of Photoshop.If you are into creating music, try out some of the tracker software such as ProTracker, or AHX for unique chip sounds.For young people learning to code, AMOS is a fun and powerful language to start with. Something that could transition into C++ later on.Another nice tool was Dir Opus, file-handling made easy and logical. I wish Microsoft or Apple would have picked it up back in the days....

In a recent development, ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.
